items.content: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data? Ethan Lin † † thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: Cornell University Akanksha Sarkar 1 1 1 Project website: https://codiscovery.ai/AgentSSL Affiliation: Cornell University Ziang Liu Affiliation: Cornell University Kristin Branson Affiliation: Howard Hughes Medical Institute Jennifer J. Sun Affiliation: Cornell University Abstract Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning ( AgentSSL ), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent’s feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench , a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks. 2 2 footnotetext: Selection Benchmark: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ethan-y-lin/ProgramSelectBench 1 Introduction Figure 1 : MLE Agent research is focused on reducing engineering cost, but relies on human labeled data. SSL research seeks to reduce annotation effort but requires human engineering to deploy. We study whether AgentSSL can reduce both costs. “What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.” — Werner Heisenberg Modern machine learning depends on two costly inputs: (1) labeled data to provide supervision, and (2) human engineering to design the inductive biases and pipelines (e.g. architectures, augmentations, and training strategies) required to extract signal from that data Hestness et al. (2017) ; Kaplan et al. (2020) . Recent agent-based approaches target engineering cost by reframing ML pipeline development as program search, iteratively generating and refining executable code based on task feedback. The capabilities of these agents have improved significantly. For example, on MLE-Bench Chan et al. (2024) , a benchmark of 75 Kaggle competitions, the top agent performance has risen from a mean percentile rank of 45.2% Toledo et al. (2025) to 83.1% Hambardzumyan et al. (2026) in just a single year, driven by a rapidly expanding ecosystem of agents Jiang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Nam et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) ; Hambardzumyan et al. (2026) . Despite this success, there remains a fundamental limitation in our method of questioning : existing agentic benchmarks overwhelmingly assume fully supervised settings. MLE-Bench primarily contains tasks with thousands to millions of training samples. As a result, agents are optimized to search over programs under the assumption that labeled data is abundant. This assumption rarely holds in practice. In many real-world domains (including scientific discovery, medical diagnostics, and environmental monitoring), labeled data is scarce and expensive while unlabeled data is abundant. This raises a fundamental question: can agent-based systems remain effective in data-scarce regimes by leveraging unlabeled data? This places the problem naturally within semi-supervised learning (SSL), where a small labeled set is paired with a much larger unlabeled corpus. Despite strong results on classical benchmarks such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 Krizhevsky and Hinton (2009) , SSL remains difficult to deploy in practice since these methods are highly sensitive to how well the data distribution matches the algorithm’s underlying assumptions (e.g. cluster structure, consistency under augmentation, etc.) Zhu (2005a) ; Yang et al. (2023) . As a result, the methods often require significant dataset-specific tuning. This brittleness suggests that deploying SSL can be viewed as a search problem over a large design space spanning graph-based label propagation Zhu (2005a) , pseudo-labeling Lee (2013) , consistency regularization Tarvainen and Valpola (2017) , and many more Zhu (2005a) ; Yang et al. (2023) . In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL) , formulating the domain-specific application of SSL as a program search problem. We decompose this problem into two core challenges: (1) program discovery , where agents must discover effective SSL programs under limited feedback, and (2) program selection , where a single program must be identified from the discovered candidates without a large labeled validation set. To study program discovery, we investigate two unsupervised feedback approaches for guiding agentic search. We find that, even when unsupervised feedback is weakly or even negatively correlated with final accuracy, agents can still discover SSL programs that are competitive with, and in 8 of 12 settings outperform , recent SSL baselines. Through extensive empirical and qualitative analysis, we find that agents explore and combine diverse ideas spanning decades of SSL research, with the strongest agent-generated solutions effectively leveraging both unlabeled data and domain-specific structure. Despite discovering strong SSL programs, agents face a significant challenge in reliably selecting the best programs. This reflects a longstanding challenge in practical SSL: selecting methods and hyperparameters without access to a reliable labeled validation set Oliver et al. (2019) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . We evaluate two promising approaches. First, we find that unsupervised metrics enable effective selection when underlying assumptions hold. Second, when unsupervised metrics fail, actively allocating labels to program selection can outperform allocating them to training. To facilitate further research, we introduce ProgramSelectBench (Appendix C ), a large-scale program selection benchmark comprising 16,977 precomputed programs representing over 10,000 GPU hours of compute. Finally, we evaluate AgentSSL on animal detection tasks from real-world ecology pipelines, showing both its potential to reduce annotation cost and the instability of deploying agent-discovered SSL strategies outside controlled classification benchmarks. To summarize, our contributions are: • We introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), formulating SSL as agentic search over the space of SSL programs. • We show that MLE agents can autonomously discover diverse, domain-adapted SSL programs that effectively leverage unlabeled data, achieving performance competitive with established SSL baselines, outperforming them in 8 of 12 settings. • We identify reliable program selection as an open problem for AgentSSL, and release ProgramSelectBench , a large-scale program selection benchmark with 16,977 programs of human baseline and agent solutions. • We evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, demonstrating the potential and challenges for agents to reduce annotation-cost in practice. 2 Related Work 2.1 Automating Machine Learning Engineering (MLE) Automating MLE has long been a goal of the ML community. Traditional AutoML methods, including hyperparameter optimization Akiba et al. (2019) , pipeline search Olson and Moore (2019) , and neural architecture search (NAS) White et al. (2023) ; He et al. (2021) , typically formulate automation as optimization over predefined search spaces, such as model architectures, training procedures, and hyperparameters. While effective in many settings, these methods often require substantial human specification of the search space and optimization objective. Recent LLM-based MLE agents offer a more flexible alternative by searching over executable programs and iteratively proposing, executing, debugging, and refining code using feedback from the environment Novikov et al. (2025) ; Jiang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Nam et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) ; Hambardzumyan et al. (2026) . Because these agents combine many interacting design choices, controlled evaluation frameworks are important for isolating the effects of search policies, feedback signals, and other components Toledo et al. (2025) ; Yang et al. (2025) . We use Aira-Dojo Toledo et al. (2025) as such a test harness, providing a consistent environment for studying these design choices in our SSL setting. Existing MLE agents are also typically evaluated on supervised-learning benchmarks with substantial labeled training and validation data. MLE-Bench Chan et al. (2024) evaluates agents across 75 Kaggle competitions, while AIRS-Bench Lupidi et al. (2026) considers challenging tasks drawn from ML research papers. In contrast, we evaluate MLE agents in a data-efficient setting where labeled data is limited, making program discovery and program selection under weak feedback itself a central challenge. 2.2 Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) SSL studies how to leverage unlabeled data together with limited labeled data. We briefly review its major paradigms since our agent builds on both traditional and modern SSL methods. Classical SSL methods. Classical methods impose assumptions on how labeled and unlabeled examples should relate Zhu (2005b) . For example, graph-based methods encourage connected examples on a similarity graph to share labels Song et al. (2021) ; low-density separation methods, such as transductive SVMs, encourage decision boundaries to avoid dense regions Chapelle and Zien (2005) . Deep SSL methods. Deep SSL implements similar assumptions through neural training objectives Yang et al. (2023) . Pseudo-labeling and self-training use model predictions on unlabeled data as targets. Consistency regularization enforces invariance to augmentations. Early methods like Π \Pi -Model Laine and Aila (2017) and Mean Teacher Tarvainen and Valpola (2018) used consistency between different trained networks as an objective. FixMatch Sohn et al. (2020) combines several SSL approaches, including weakly augmented pseudo-labeling, confidence thresholding, and strongly augmented consistency training. Subsequent methods such as SoftMatch Chen et al. (2023) refine this through adaptive thresholds, curriculum selection, or confidence weighting. FineSSL and V-PET are recent SSL methods tailored for foundation models, either through addressing biases in foundation-model adaptation Gan and Wei (2024) or ensembling complementary pseudolabels from multiple PEFT methods and foundation-model backbones Zhang et al. (2025) . 2.3 Unsupervised and Active Model Selection Model selection without a large labeled validation set remains an open challenge in data-efficient settings. Unsupervised model selection replaces labeled validation performance with statistics computed from model predictions or learned representations. Many such metrics were originally developed in other contexts, including classical clustering and statistics Fowlkes and Mallows (1983) ; Vinh et al. (2009) ; Halkidi et al. (2002) ; Caliński and Harabasz (1974) , representation learning Garrido et al. (2023) , and domain adaptation or data-efficient learning Cui et al. (2020) ; Saito et al. (2021) . Recent work has repurposed and evaluated these signals as unsupervised validation criteria in unsupervised domain adaptation Ericsson et al. (2023) and SSL Zhang et al. (2025) , but their reliability depends on assumptions that may not hold consistently across datasets or models Kay et al. (2025) ; Ericsson et al. (2023) . An orthogonal direction is active model selection , which uses a limited annotation budget to identify the best model. Existing approaches include uncertainty- or variance-driven methods that prioritize labels most useful for reducing uncertainty in model performance estimates Kossen et al. (2021) ; Matsuura and Hara (2023) , as well as probabilistic approaches that model uncertainty over candidate model quality and use this posterior to guide label acquisition Kay et al. (2025) ; Okanovic et al. (2024) . Both directions provide promising avenues for improving model selection in AgentSSL when a large labeled validation set is unavailable. Benchmarking model selection. Existing evaluations of model selection under limited supervision remains limited, both in size and diversity of candidate models. In particular, active model selection methods are typically evaluated over a finite set derived from following the same fine-tuning procedure on different pre-trained models and hyperparameters Okanovic et al. (2024) ; Kay et al. (2025) . This leaves open how well existing selection methods scale to settings where candidate solutions may differ substantially in architectures, training procedures, and hyperparameters. 3 Problem Setup Figure 2 : Overview of AgentSSL. Given a small labeled set and a larger unlabeled corpus, an LLM-based agent generates SSL programs that are evaluated using either unsupervised SSL metrics or noisy validation feedback, with the resulting fitness score guiding iterative refinement. Following search, we must select the best program either using unsupervised metrics or active model selection. We evaluate AgentSSL on both image classification SSL benchmarks and real-world ecological detection tasks. 3.1 SSL Problem Formulation In the SSL setting, each task provides a labeled dataset L = { ( x i ℓ , y i ℓ ) } i = 1 | L | L=\{(x_{i}^{\ell},y_{i}^{\ell})\}_{i=1}^{|L|} and an unlabeled dataset U = { x i u } i = 1 | U | , U=\{x_{i}^{u}\}_{i=1}^{|U|}, where typically | L | ≪ | U | |L|\ll|U| with the goal of constructing a prediction function h : 𝒳 → Y h:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow Y that achieves high performance on a held-out test distribution. Rather than restricting the solution space to a particular parameterized model trained with a fixed SSL objective, we define a solution more generally as a program 𝒜 : ( L , U ) ↦ h , \mathcal{A}:(L,U)\mapsto h, which takes the labeled and unlabeled data as input and returns a predictor. This formulation includes conventional deep SSL methods that learn parameters θ \theta of a model f θ f_{\theta} using both L L and U U , while also allowing broader strategies such as classical transductive or graph-based SSL methods. 3.2 AgentSSL Problem Formulation We formulate AgentSSL as an agentic search problem over the space of SSL programs, comprising two core challenges: (1) program discovery , where an agent iteratively generates and refines candidate programs under limited feedback, and (2) program selection , where a single program must be identified from the discovered candidates for deployment under label scarcity. Program Discovery . We define the solution space as a set of programs 𝒮 = { 𝒜 : ( L , U ) ↦ h } \mathcal{S}=\{\mathcal{A}:(L,U)\mapsto h\} , where each program specifies a complete learning procedure for constructing a predictor from the available data. Following prior work Toledo et al. (2025) , we model agentic search as growth of a directed acyclic graph over programs: greedy and MCTS expand single nodes and induce trees, while evolutionary crossover combines two parents into one child. At iteration t t , the agent maintains a directed graph G t = ( V t , E t ) , G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t}), where each node v ∈ V t ⊆ 𝒮 v\in V_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{S} represents a candidate SSL program and each directed edge ( v i , v j ) ∈ E t (v_{i},v_{j})\in E_{t} represents a transformation from one program to another. At each iteration, the agent selects one or more existing programs, applies an operator to produce a new candidate program, evaluates it using a feedback signal, and adds the resulting node to the search graph. Concretely, an AgentSSL search procedure is specified by the tuple ( F , π sel , 𝒪 , π op , M ) , \left(F,\pi_{\mathrm{sel}},\mathcal{O},\pi_{\mathrm{op}},M\right), where F F is a fitness function, π sel \pi_{\mathrm{sel}} is a node selection policy, 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is a set of program transformation operators, π op \pi_{\mathrm{op}} is an operator selection policy, and M M is the LLM. We use a fixed operator set with Draft, Debug, Improve, and Analyze operators (Appendix H.1 ). Program Selection . Following program discovery, we obtain a pool of candidate programs 𝒫 ⊆ 𝒮 \mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{S} . The goal of program selection is to identify the best-performing program 𝒜 ∗ ∈ 𝒫 \mathcal{A}^{*}\in\mathcal{P} , defined as 𝒜 ∗ = arg ⁡ max 𝒜 ∈ 𝒫 ⁡ 𝒬 ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) , \mathcal{A}^{*}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{P}}\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{A}), where 𝒬 ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{A}) denotes the performance of the predictor produced by program 𝒜 \mathcal{A} on the test distribution. However, true performance is unknown, and the limited labeled data available in SSL makes it difficult to reliably identify 𝒜 ∗ \mathcal{A}^{*} . We therefore study program selection under different information constraints. Unsupervised selection chooses programs using label-free metrics Zhang et al. (2025) computed on an unlabelled validation set. Active model selection chooses programs by actively querying a limited number of test labels. Evaluation . We evaluate these two challenges separately. To assess program discovery, we measure oracle performance , defined as the test performance of the best program in the discovered pool, 𝒬 ⁡ ( 𝒜 ∗ ) \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{A}^{*}) . This measures the quality of the best discovered solution, independent of our ability to select it. To assess program selection, we measure selection regret , defined as R sel = 𝒬 ⁡ ( 𝒜 ∗ ) − 𝒬 ⁡ ( 𝒜 s ) , R_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{A}^{*})-\mathcal{Q}({\mathcal{A}}_{s}), where 𝒜 s {\mathcal{A}}_{s} is the program chosen by a selection method. Lower regret indicates that the selection method more reliably identifies high performing programs from the discovered pool. 3.3 Agent Design Space The AgentSSL formulation exposes several design choices that can affect how agents explore the space of SSL programs. We focus on three components that are especially relevant to our study: the fitness function, the search strategy, and the language model. Fitness Functions ( F F ). The fitness function defines the feedback signal received by the agent during search. This is especially important in SSL, where labeled validation data is scarce. We consider two families of feedback signals: (i) noisy validation , where a small labeled subset is held out for evaluation, and (ii) unsupervised metrics , Zhu (2005a) ; Chapelle et al. (2009) ; Zhang et al. (2025) where programs are scored using label-free statistics computed from predictions or representations on unlabeled data. Noisy validation provides direct supervised feedback but can have high variance in low-label regimes. Unsupervised metrics instead test whether agents can search effectively using only structure in unlabeled data. The construction of the noisy validation signal introduces a tradeoff between robustness and evaluation cost: stronger estimates such as cross-validation reduce variance but substantially increase program evaluation time. In our experiments, we tune this configuration separately for each dataset, though we view automated adaptation of this tradeoff as an interesting direction for future work. More details about the metric calculation in Appendix A.2 . Search Strategies ( π sel \pi_{\mathrm{sel}} ). The search policy π sel \pi_{\mathrm{sel}} determines which nodes v ∈ V t v\in V_{t} in the search graph G t = ( V t , E t ) G_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t}) are expanded at each iteration. Different strategies induce different exploration–exploitation tradeoffs: greedy selects the highest-score programs under F F , evolutionary search mutates a population of candidate programs, and MCTS balances exploration and exploitation through tree search. We study how π sel \pi_{\mathrm{sel}} affects performance and diversity of discovered SSL strategies. Language Model Backbone ( M M ). The language model M M instantiates the program transformation operators 𝒪 \mathcal{O} by generating modifications to existing programs. items.raw_text: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data? Ethan Lin † † thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: Cornell University Akanksha Sarkar 1 1 1 Project website: https://codiscovery.ai/AgentSSL Affiliation: Cornell University Ziang Liu Affiliation: Cornell University Kristin Branson Affiliation: Howard Hughes Medical Institute Jennifer J. Sun Affiliation: Cornell University Abstract Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning ( AgentSSL ), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent’s feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench , a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks. 2 2 footnotetext: Selection Benchmark: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ethan-y-lin/ProgramSelectBench 1 Introduction Figure 1 : MLE Agent research is focused on reducing engineering cost, but relies on human labeled data. SSL research seeks to reduce annotation effort but requires human engineering to deploy. We study whether AgentSSL can reduce both costs. “What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.” — Werner Heisenberg Modern machine learning depends on two costly inputs: (1) labeled data to provide supervision, and (2) human engineering to design the inductive biases and pipelines (e.g. architectures, augmentations, and training strategies) required to extract signal from that data Hestness et al. (2017) ; Kaplan et al. (2020) . Recent agent-based approaches target engineering cost by reframing ML pipeline development as program search, iteratively generating and refining executable code based on task feedback. The capabilities of these agents have improved significantly. For example, on MLE-Bench Chan et al. (2024) , a benchmark of 75 Kaggle competitions, the top agent performance has risen from a mean percentile rank of 45.2% Toledo et al. (2025) to 83.1% Hambardzumyan et al. (2026) in just a single year, driven by a rapidly expanding ecosystem of agents Jiang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Nam et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) ; Hambardzumyan et al. (2026) . Despite this success, there remains a fundamental limitation in our method of questioning : existing agentic benchmarks overwhelmingly assume fully supervised settings. MLE-Bench primarily contains tasks with thousands to millions of training samples. As a result, agents are optimized to search over programs under the assumption that labeled data is abundant. This assumption rarely holds in practice. In many real-world domains (including scientific discovery, medical diagnostics, and environmental monitoring), labeled data is scarce and expensive while unlabeled data is abundant. This raises a fundamental question: can agent-based systems remain effective in data-scarce regimes by leveraging unlabeled data? This places the problem naturally within semi-supervised learning (SSL), where a small labeled set is paired with a much larger unlabeled corpus. Despite strong results on classical benchmarks such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 Krizhevsky and Hinton (2009) , SSL remains difficult to deploy in practice since these methods are highly sensitive to how well the data distribution matches the algorithm’s underlying assumptions (e.g. cluster structure, consistency under augmentation, etc.) Zhu (2005a) ; Yang et al. (2023) . As a result, the methods often require significant dataset-specific tuning. This brittleness suggests that deploying SSL can be viewed as a search problem over a large design space spanning graph-based label propagation Zhu (2005a) , pseudo-labeling Lee (2013) , consistency regularization Tarvainen and Valpola (2017) , and many more Zhu (2005a) ; Yang et al. (2023) . In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL) , formulating the domain-specific application of SSL as a program search problem. We decompose this problem into two core challenges: (1) program discovery , where agents must discover effective SSL programs under limited feedback, and (2) program selection , where a single program must be identified from the discovered candidates without a large labeled validation set. To study program discovery, we investigate two unsupervised feedback approaches for guiding agentic search. We find that, even when unsupervised feedback is weakly or even negatively correlated with final accuracy, agents can still discover SSL programs that are competitive with, and in 8 of 12 settings outperform , recent SSL baselines. Through extensive empirical and qualitative analysis, we find that agents explore and combine diverse ideas spanning decades of SSL research, with the strongest agent-generated solutions effectively leveraging both unlabeled data and domain-specific structure. Despite discovering strong SSL programs, agents face a significant challenge in reliably selecting the best programs. This reflects a longstanding challenge in practical SSL: selecting methods and hyperparameters without access to a reliable labeled validation set Oliver et al. (2019) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . We evaluate two promising approaches. First, we find that unsupervised metrics enable effective selection when underlying assumptions hold. Second, when unsupervised metrics fail, actively allocating labels to program selection can outperform allocating them to training. To facilitate further research, we introduce ProgramSelectBench (Appendix C ), a large-scale program selection benchmark comprising 16,977 precomputed programs representing over 10,000 GPU hours of compute. Finally, we evaluate AgentSSL on animal detection tasks from real-world ecology pipelines, showing both its potential to reduce annotation cost and the instability of deploying agent-discovered SSL strategies outside controlled classification benchmarks. To summarize, our contributions are: • We introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), formulating SSL as agentic search over the space of SSL programs. • We show that MLE agents can autonomously discover diverse, domain-adapted SSL programs that effectively leverage unlabeled data, achieving performance competitive with established SSL baselines, outperforming them in 8 of 12 settings. • We identify reliable program selection as an open problem for AgentSSL, and release ProgramSelectBench , a large-scale program selection benchmark with 16,977 programs of human baseline and agent solutions. • We evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, demonstrating the potential and challenges for agents to reduce annotation-cost in practice. 2 Related Work 2.1 Automating Machine Learning Engineering (MLE) Automating MLE has long been a goal of the ML community. Traditional AutoML methods, including hyperparameter optimization Akiba et al. (2019) , pipeline search Olson and Moore (2019) , and neural architecture search (NAS) White et al. (2023) ; He et al. (2021) , typically formulate automation as optimization over predefined search spaces, such as model architectures, training procedures, and hyperparameters. While effective in many settings, these methods often require substantial human specification of the search space and optimization objective. Recent LLM-based MLE agents offer a more flexible alternative by searching over executable programs and iteratively proposing, executing, debugging, and refining code using feedback from the environment Novikov et al. (2025) ; Jiang et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Nam et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2026) ; Hambardzumyan et al. (2026) . Because these agents combine many interacting design choices, controlled evaluation frameworks are important for isolating the effects of search policies, feedback signals, and other components Toledo et al. (2025) ; Yang et al. (2025) . We use Aira-Dojo Toledo et al. (2025) as such a test harness, providing a consistent environment for studying these design choices in our SSL setting. Existing MLE agents are also typically evaluated on supervised-learning benchmarks with substantial labeled training and validation data. MLE-Bench Chan et al. (2024) evaluates agents across 75 Kaggle competitions, while AIRS-Bench Lupidi et al. (2026) considers challenging tasks drawn from ML research papers. In contrast, we evaluate MLE agents in a data-efficient setting where labeled data is limited, making program discovery and program selection under weak feedback itself a central challenge. 2.2 Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) SSL studies how to leverage unlabeled data together with limited labeled data. We briefly review its major paradigms since our agent builds on both traditional and modern SSL methods. Classical SSL methods. Classical methods impose assumptions on how labeled and unlabeled examples should relate Zhu (2005b) . For example, graph-based methods encourage connected examples on a similarity graph to share labels Song et al. (2021) ; low-density separation methods, such as transductive SVMs, encourage decision boundaries to avoid dense regions Chapelle and Zien (2005) . Deep SSL methods. Deep SSL implements similar assumptions through neural training objectives Yang et al. (2023) . Pseudo-labeling and self-training use model predictions on unlabeled data as targets. Consistency regularization enforces invariance to augmentations. Early methods like Π \Pi -Model Laine and Aila (2017) and Mean Teacher Tarvainen and Valpola (2018) used consistency between different trained networks as an objective. FixMatch Sohn et al. (2020) combines several SSL approaches, including weakly augmented pseudo-labeling, confidence thresholding, and strongly augmented consistency training. Subsequent methods such as SoftMatch Chen et al. (2023) refine this through adaptive thresholds, curriculum selection, or confidence weighting. FineSSL and V-PET are recent SSL methods tailored for foundation models, either through addressing biases in foundation-model adaptation Gan and Wei (2024) or ensembling complementary pseudolabels from multiple PEFT methods and foundation-model backbones Zhang et al. (2025) . 2.3 Unsupervised and Active Model Selection Model selection without a large labeled validation set remains an open challenge in data-efficient settings. Unsupervised model selection replaces labeled validation performance with statistics computed from model predictions or learned representations. Many such metrics were originally developed in other contexts, including classical clustering and statistics Fowlkes and Mallows (1983) ; Vinh et al. (2009) ; Halkidi et al. (2002) ; Caliński and Harabasz (1974) , representation learning Garrido et al. (2023) , and domain adaptation or data-efficient learning Cui et al. (2020) ; Saito et al. (2021) . Recent work has repurposed and evaluated these signals as unsupervised validation criteria in unsupervised domain adaptation Ericsson et al. (2023) and SSL Zhang et al. (2025) , but their reliability depends on assumptions that may not hold consistently across datasets or models Kay et al. (2025) ; Ericsson et al. (2023) . An orthogonal direction is active model selection , which uses a limited annotation budget to identify the best model. Existing approaches include uncertainty- or variance-driven methods that prioritize labels most useful for reducing uncertainty in model performance estimates Kossen et al. (2021) ; Matsuura and Hara (2023) , as well as probabilistic approaches that model uncertainty over candidate model quality and use this posterior to guide label acquisition Kay et al. (2025) ; Okanovic et al. (2024) . Both directions provide promising avenues for improving model selection in AgentSSL when a large labeled validation set is unavailable. Benchmarking model selection. Existing evaluations of model selection under limited supervision remains limited, both in size and diversity of candidate models. In particular, active model selection methods are typically evaluated over a finite set derived from following the same fine-tuning procedure on different pre-trained models and hyperparameters Okanovic et al. (2024) ; Kay et al. (2025) . This leaves open how well existing selection methods scale to settings where candidate solutions may differ substantially in architectures, training procedures, and hyperparameters. 3 Problem Setup Figure 2 : Overview of AgentSSL. Given a small labeled set and a larger unlabeled corpus, an LLM-based agent generates SSL programs that are evaluated using either unsupervised SSL metrics or noisy validation feedback, with the resulting fitness score guiding iterative refinement. items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details Distributional Alignment Games for Answer-Level Fine-Tuning Mehryar Mohri Jon Schneider Yifan Wu ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract We focus on the problem of \emph{Answer-Level Fine-Tuning} (ALFT), where the goal is to optimize a language model based on the correctness or properties of its final answers, rather than the specific reasoning traces used to produce them. Directly optimizing answer-level objectives is computationally intractable due to the need to marginalize over the vast space of latent reasoning paths. To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a \emph{Distributional Alignment Game}. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. View details Rational Transductors Mehryar Mohri ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract Standard Transformers excel at semantic modeling but struggle with rigid sequential logic and state tracking, fundamentally limited to AC0 complexity without intermediate chain-of- thought. In this work, we introduce Rational Transductors, a dual-stream architecture that augments the Transformer with a linear, matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA). By injecting rational state information into the attention mechanism via a Deep Rational Injection scheme, our framework strictly generalizes the expressive power of Transformers to capture all Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems (such as Parity and Modular Counting) while preserving O(log T) parallel training efficiency. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. View details Distributional Alignment Games for Answer-Level Fine-Tuning Mehryar Mohri Jon Schneider Yifan Wu ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract We focus on the problem of \emph{Answer-Level Fine-Tuning} (ALFT), where the goal is to optimize a language model based on the correctness or properties of its final answers, rather than the specific reasoning traces used to produce them. Directly optimizing answer-level objectives is computationally intractable due to the need to marginalize over the vast space of latent reasoning paths. To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a \emph{Distributional Alignment Game}. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. View details Rational Transductors Mehryar Mohri ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract Standard Transformers excel at semantic modeling but struggle with rigid sequential logic and state tracking, fundamentally limited to AC0 complexity without intermediate chain-of- thought. In this work, we introduce Rational Transductors, a dual-stream architecture that augments the Transformer with a linear, matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA). By injecting rational state information into the attention mechanism via a Deep Rational Injection scheme, our framework strictly generalizes the expressive power of Transformers to capture all Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems (such as Parity and Modular Counting) while preserving O(log T) parallel training efficiency. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. Grounding in real world signals To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates. Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions. SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization. Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. Industry specific simulation We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. Automated query generation While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. The six-stage pipeline Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. PODCAST SERIES The AI Revolution in Medicine, Revisited Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine. Listen now Opens in a new tab Privacy and safety by design Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Results and impact Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs. On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure. Conclusion As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety. Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next. At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale . Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets ! items.raw_text: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful.
