O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates. Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions. SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization. Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. Industry specific simulation We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. Automated query generation While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. The six-stage pipeline Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. Simulation / Modeling / Design Run GPU-Powered Black Hole Interferometry with NVIDIA cuPhoton Nov 13, 2026 By Akhilesh Mishra and Quynh L. Nguyen Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA cuPhoton .xBeam accelerates radio interferometry correlation for the Event Horizon Telescope by processing voltage recordings into visibilities on GPUs. The FX correlator ingests VDIF frames, applies delay and fringe corrections, channelizes signals via FFT, cross-multiplies station pairs, and writes visibilities in DiFX SWIN or xbeam-v1 format. On an NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 system with 64 GPUs and GPUDirect Storage, xBeam correlated a 10 TB dataset in 70 seconds, achieving a 460x speedup over an x86 CPU baseline of 31,992 seconds. Scaling splits observation time across GPUs using --devices on a single node or --shard-count and --shard-index across nodes, with merge-shards combining partial SWIN outputs into a complete visibility set. AI agents can orchestrate end-to-end pipelines by parsing VDIF metadata, generating JSON job specifications, launching xBeam correlation across GPU clusters, and monitoring execution. Next Steps Explore the NVIDIA cuPhoton repository for imaging modules, xBeam, and sample recordings with job files. Read the Faster Scientific Image Analysis with NVIDIA cuPhoton walkthrough for an imaging-focused tutorial. Review the NVIDIA cuPhoton product page for additional resources and related examples. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Imaging black holes is challenging because they are distant and appear tiny in the sky—for example, M87*’s observed ring spans just 42 microarcseconds. The black hole itself emits no light, so telescopes capture radio emission from superheated gas swirling outside the event horizon. The black hole’s intense gravity bends the paths of this light, shaping the bright ring that frames the central shadow. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) addresses this challenge by linking 13 radio observatory stations across locations, including Hawaii, Chile, Spain, Mexico, and the South Pole, through very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI). These stations record millimeter and submillimeter radio signals as high-speed voltage streams, which are synchronized and combined to reconstruct detailed images. The next-generation EHT (ngEHT) aims to add observing sites to improve image quality and track changes around black holes over time. This post walks through GPU-based interferometry with cuPhoton.xBeam, from reading telescope recordings to generating visibilities and scaling across multiple GPUs. These measurements serve as inputs to downstream calibration and image reconstruction, which are outside the scope of this tutorial. Figure 1. Radio telescopes record signals that are correlated into visibilities for image reconstruction. Conceptual illustration NVIDIA cuPhoton .xBeam performs GPU-based correlation for interferometry and organizes recorded data for parallel reads. It correlates signals from pairs of telescopes to produce one complex visibility for each pair of stations, each frequency channel, and each short time interval. The next step can involve constructing a 3D gas model from these visibilities via a distinct downstream process, such as Gaussian splatting. This method models the emitting gas as numerous compact, glowing blobs moving along orbits near a spinning black hole, optimized to match the observed visibilities. cuPhoton does not currently incorporate this second component. The NVIDIA cuPhoton team collaborates with the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and the MIT Haystack Observatory to accelerate data ingestion and correlation using xBeam. Running on an NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 system with 64 GPUs and GPUDirect Storage (GDS) in compatibility mode, xBeam processed a 10 TB dataset in 70 seconds —about 460x faster than an x86 CPU baseline of 31,992 seconds (8.89 hours). The sky is an inverse problem The EHT records radio signals in two polarizations at up to 64 gigabits per second per telescope, generating petabytes of data. Correlating signals between telescope pairs produces visibilities, which sample Fourier components of the sky’s brightness. Earth’s rotation traces sparse measurement tracks, and reconstruction algorithms combine these samples into an image. Rapid changes in sources such as Sgr A* complicate this process because observations capture an evolving source over time. An Earth-sized array observing at 1.3 mm only collects (u, v) measurements along the elliptical tracks drawn by Earth’s rotation. Because no physical lens forms the image directly, reconstructive algorithms must solve an inverse problem to synthesize the picture from sparse samples. For targets like Sgr A*, the source changes during an observation session, complicating reconstruction methods that assume a static source ( Focus on First Sgr A* Results ). Figure 2 shows the imaging workflow using a synthetic source. The left panel shows the (u, v) tracks that an array laid out like the 2017 EHT samples over one night as Earth turns. The next panel shows visibility amplitudes, |V(u, v)| plotted against baseline length, followed by a dirty image formed from the sparse samples. The right panel shows a crescent model, a simple ring-shaped image that researchers can fit to those amplitudes. Figure 2. Synthetic EHT-like example showing spatial-frequency sampling, visibility amplitudes, a dirty image, and a crescent model Light passing near a black hole can orbit it before escaping, forming a thin photon ring near the shadow’s edge. Its size and shape can help constrain the black hole’s mass, spin, and viewing angle, while its interferometric signal produces characteristic oscillations. The proposed Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) aims to measure this ring, and future ngEHT observations at 345 GHz could detect its signature through polarization measurements. What cuPhoton.xBeam computes cuPhoton.xBeam is the FX correlator in the cuPhoton toolkit. It restructures the recordings so they can be read in parallel, builds a .vdix index so later reads jump straight to each frame, and loads the voltages into GPU memory. Then it does the FX work, like DiFX (CPU-based, open-source software correlator): it Fourier-transforms each station’s voltage into frequency channels (F) and cross-multiplies the station and polarization pairs at each frequency channel requested by the job (X). Those steps run on the GPU. In order, xBeam does five things: 1. Ingest . Read the VDIF frames and place each one at its correct time. xBeam builds a small index file, the .vdix sidecar, that records where every frame is without copying the data, so later reads jump straight to the right place. xBeam indexes VDIF frames by timestamp, thread, and physical location. Its .vdix sidecars let subsequent reads locate the required data without rewriting the recording. Missing or invalid data remain explicitly tracked. 2. Delay and fringe . Shift each station’s samples by the delay in the job’s model, so the same wavefront lines up at every station, and remove the phase drift caused by Earth’s motion. Learn more Imaging black holes is challenging because they are distant and appear tiny in the sky—for example, M87*’s observed ring spans just 42 microarcseconds. items.content: Back to Articles Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software Enterprise Article Published October 29, 2026 Upvote 36 +30 Kate Soule katesoule Follow ibm-granite Luis A Lastras GrizleeBer Follow ibm-granite Subhajit Chaudhury subhajit1412 Follow ibm-granite Abraham Daniels abedaniels Follow ibm-granite Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1 , showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo. items.content: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 17 +11 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review. To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model : pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git" hf auth login tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to '' It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space . Random vs Overfit With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path. So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study , the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24. That gives us two ways to build the weights: Start with random weights and a fixed seed. Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris". The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed. So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both. Open questions As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet: How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays? How often does it send us chasing false alarms? How much work do baseline reviews take? We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss. Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for. Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs. Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space , try the tmic workflow , and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract. items.content: Back to Articles A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks. Published November 5, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 40 +34 Olesia Krizhevich olesiagradium Follow gradium Laurent Mazare lmz Follow gradium Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you. We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard. Why a voice should live on your device Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate. Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both. We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design. Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages. What we released Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes. It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license. Demos and first projects The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page. The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one. Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it. Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face. How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub , the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility ( word error rate of the outputs ), speed ( inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio ), and naturalness ( UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean ). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most. On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish , and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size. Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio. Inference We built a new inference framework, ptts , specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®). Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer , held by the processor next to the text tokenizer: from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) print ( f" {model.num_parameters():,} " ) # 30,788,354 print ( f" {processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,} " ) # 10,305,313 A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs: conversation = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Hello from Phonon." }]} ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , add_generation_prompt= True , processor_kwargs={ "audio_prompt_latents" : [voice]}, ).to(model.device) # prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|> generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio: outputs = model.generate(**inputs) # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32) audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask) processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav" ) See the docs 🤗 for more! What's next Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio . Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device. We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need. Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks. Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build. One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. items.content: Back to Articles Decision Models in Hugging Face Published November 10, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 89 +83 Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow Lysandre lysandre Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text. Consider a customer support system receiving the following message: "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers. llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0 > We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." , which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON. [Start thinking] ... [end thinking] ```json { "team_to_handle" : "Billing" , "urgency" : "High" , "request_refund" : true } But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } This is the key idea behind decision models . What are decision models? A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands. TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2). The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models ) For a decision model, the fundamental interface is: State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities Why not use LLMs for everything? We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks. However, there are a few problems with this approach. LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices. Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work. Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work. How are decision models different from classification models? Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification. Traditional classification Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments: Billing Technical support Sales A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution. The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head . If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model. Zero-shot classification Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time. For example: from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'], # 'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]} Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs. from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" , "legal" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'], # 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]} One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis. This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is. Where decision models differ Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul). More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions . Consider these three approaches: Property Classification Zero-shot classification Decision model Probability over choices Yes Yes Yes Labels defined at inference No Yes Yes Multiple typed questions No No Yes Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions Task-specific Possible with adaptation Native primitives The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions. The decision model interface A decision model request has the following two components: state questions State The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models. For example: { "customer_message" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "subscription" : "pro" , "previous_tickets" : 2 } Questions and their primitives Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions: Choice: Select one of several possible answers. Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale. Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically. Let's go over them one by one. Choice: A probability distribution over options Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification. Suppose we ask: Which department should handle this customer request? The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z 1 , … , z K z_1,\ldots,z_K z 1 ​ , … , z K ​ , (with K K K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax: p i = exp ⁡ ( z i ) ∑ j = 1 K exp ⁡ ( z j ) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} p i ​ = ∑ j = 1 K ​ exp ( z j ​ ) exp ( z i ​ ) ​ Here, K K K is the number of choices. Consider this illustrative distribution: Choice Probability Billing 0.998 Technical support 0.001 Sales 0.001 The probabilities sum to one: ∑ i = 1 K p i = 1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i = 1 ∑ K ​ p i ​ = 1. The model chooses the option with the largest probability: y ^ = arg ⁡ max ⁡ i p i \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y ^ ​ = ar g i max ​ p i ​ In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives. Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale? Consider the question: How urgent is this customer request? We define three levels: 0: Low urgency 1: Medium urgency 2: High urgency from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] }, } } ) # { # 'urgency': { # 'type': 'score', # 'score': 1.7053890228271484, # 'legend': { # '0': 'low', # '1': 'medium', # '2': 'high' # }, # 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814, # 'probabilities': { # '0': 0.014908230863511562, # '1': 0.26479458808898926, # '2': 0.7202972173690796 # } # } # } The model again produces a probability distribution: Level Probability 0 — Low 0.01 1 — Medium 0.26 2 — High 0.72 Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index . For a random variable X X X representing the level, the expectation is: E [ X ] = ∑ i = 0 K − 1 i p i \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E [ X ] = i = 0 ∑ K − 1 ​ i p i ​ For our example: E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.01 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.01 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 The reported score is therefore 1.7 . This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7. Noul: A Bernoulli decision The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question. For example: Is the customer requesting a refund? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } } ) # { # 'refund': { # 'type': 'noul', # 'noul': 0.9947046637535095 # } # } Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli). Let Y Y Y represent a binary outcome: Y ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p ) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y ∼ Bernoulli ( p ) where P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . If the model returns: { "type" : "noul" , "noul" : 0.92 } it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No. The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it. Confidence: How certain is the model? So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score. The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that. For a Choice with K K K options, the confidence is: p max ⁡ − 1 K 1 − 1 K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1 − K 1 ​ p m a x ​ − K 1 ​ ​ where p max ⁡ p_{\max} p m a x ​ is the largest predicted probability. The intuition here is: A uniform distribution has confidence 0. p max ⁡ = 1 K p_{\max} = \frac{1}{K} p m a x ​ = K 1 ​ . This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely. A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. p max ⁡ = 1 p_{\max} = 1 p m a x ​ = 1 The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence. Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation . A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once: inference engines like llama.cpp can serve any decision model through the same API the Hub can package and surface them consistently and training tools can target shared primitives instead of individual architectures The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces. 1. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model. 2. Serving with llama.cpp llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API. For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF The default server runs on port 9931. We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone . With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request. The useful property is interface compatibility. curl http://localhost: 9931 /v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF", "state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Bugs and technical issues", "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, "urgency": { "type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is the request?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"] }, "refund": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } }' 3. Discovering models on the Hugging Face Hub Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture. For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones. 4. Training decision models using Hugging Face tooling Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API. Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter: each example is a decision request (a state plus questions ) paired with the gold answer. model.decision_config.prepare_inputs turns the request into model inputs, the same way it does at inference time. the model returns one logit per option, so a choice question is trained with a plain cross-entropy loss over the options. import os; os.environ[ "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES" ]= "2" import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForDecision, Trainer, TrainingArguments checkpoint = "autotrust/JEV-9B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(checkpoint) examples = [ ( "I was charged twice. Please refund me." , "refund" ), ( "My package has not arrived." , "shipping" ), ( "The application crashes when I open it." , "technical" ), ( "I want my money back." , "refund" ), ( "Where is my delivery?" , "shipping" ), ( "I cannot log into my account." , "technical" ), ] options = { "refund" : "Billing issues and refunds" , "shipping" : "Orders and deliveries" , "technical" : "Software and account issues" , } def preprocess ( text, label ): request = { "state" : text, "questions" : { "category" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Classify the support request." , "criteria" : options, } }, } (inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs( request, tokenizer ) inputs[ "marks" ] = inputs[ "marks" ].unsqueeze( 0 ) inputs[ "num_options" ] = torch.tensor([[ len (questions[ 0 ].options)]]) inputs[ "question_type_ids" ] = torch.tensor([[ 1 ]]) # choice inputs[ "labels" ] = torch.tensor( [questions[ 0 ].options.index(label)] ) return inputs dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples] class DecisionTrainer ( Trainer ): def compute_loss ( self, model, inputs, return_outputs= False , **kwargs ): inputs = inputs.copy() labels = inputs.pop( "labels" ) logits = model(**inputs) logits = logits.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [3] -> [1, 3] loss = F.cross_entropy(logits. float (), labels) return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss trainer = DecisionTrainer( model=model, args=TrainingArguments( output_dir= "./decision-toy" , max_steps= 30 , per_device_train_batch_size= 1 , learning_rate= 1e-3 , logging_steps= 5 , save_strategy= "no" , report_to= "none" , remove_unused_columns= False , ), train_dataset=dataset, data_collator= lambda batch: batch[ 0 ], ) trainer.train() First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL ( huggingface/trl#8040 ), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open. If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head. Final thoughts Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software . Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text. Consider a customer support system receiving the following message: "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers. llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0 > We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." , which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON. [Start thinking] ... [end thinking] ```json { "team_to_handle" : "Billing" , "urgency" : "High" , "request_refund" : true } But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } This is the key idea behind decision models . What are decision models? A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands. TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2). The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models ) For a decision model, the fundamental interface is: State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities Why not use LLMs for everything? We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks. However, there are a few problems with this approach. LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices. Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work. Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work. How are decision models different from classification models? Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification. Traditional classification Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments: Billing Technical support Sales A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution. The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head . If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model. Zero-shot classification Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time. For example: from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'], # 'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]} Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs. from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" , "legal" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'], # 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]} One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis. This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is. Where decision models differ Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul). More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions . Consider these three approaches: Property Classification Zero-shot classification Decision model Probability over choices Yes Yes Yes Labels defined at inference No Yes Yes Multiple typed questions No No Yes Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions Task-specific Possible with adaptation Native primitives The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions. The decision model interface A decision model request has the following two components: state questions State The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models. For example: { "customer_message" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "subscription" : "pro" , "previous_tickets" : 2 } Questions and their primitives Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions: Choice: Select one of several possible answers. Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale. Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically. Let's go over them one by one. Choice: A probability distribution over options Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification. Suppose we ask: Which department should handle this customer request? The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z 1 , … , z K z_1,\ldots,z_K z 1 ​ , … , z K ​ , (with K K K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax: p i = exp ⁡ ( z i ) ∑ j = 1 K exp ⁡ ( z j ) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} p i ​ = ∑ j = 1 K ​ exp ( z j ​ ) exp ( z i ​ ) ​ Here, K K K is the number of choices. Consider this illustrative distribution: Choice Probability Billing 0.998 Technical support 0.001 Sales 0.001 The probabilities sum to one: ∑ i = 1 K p i = 1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i = 1 ∑ K ​ p i ​ = 1. The model chooses the option with the largest probability: y ^ = arg ⁡ max ⁡ i p i \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y ^ ​ = ar g i max ​ p i ​ In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives. Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale? Consider the question: How urgent is this customer request? We define three levels: 0: Low urgency 1: Medium urgency 2: High urgency from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] }, } } ) # { # 'urgency': { # 'type': 'score', # 'score': 1.7053890228271484, # 'legend': { # '0': 'low', # '1': 'medium', # '2': 'high' # }, # 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814, # 'probabilities': { # '0': 0.014908230863511562, # '1': 0.26479458808898926, # '2': 0.7202972173690796 # } # } # } The model again produces a probability distribution: Level Probability 0 — Low 0.01 1 — Medium 0.26 2 — High 0.72 Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index . It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter: each example is a decision request (a state plus questions ) paired with the gold answer. model.decision_config.prepare_inputs turns the request into model inputs, the same way it does at inference time. the model returns one logit per option, so a choice question is trained with a plain cross-entropy loss over the options. import os; os.environ[ "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES" ]= "2" import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForDecision, Trainer, TrainingArguments checkpoint = "autotrust/JEV-9B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(checkpoint) examples = [ ( "I was charged twice. Please refund me." , "refund" ), ( "My package has not arrived." , "shipping" ), ( "The application crashes when I open it." , "technical" ), ( "I want my money back." , "refund" ), ( "Where is my delivery?" , "shipping" ), ( "I cannot log into my account." , "technical" ), ] options = { "refund" : "Billing issues and refunds" , "shipping" : "Orders and deliveries" , "technical" : "Software and account issues" , } def preprocess ( text, label ): request = { "state" : text, "questions" : { "category" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Classify the support request." , "criteria" : options, } }, } (inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs( request, tokenizer ) inputs[ "marks" ] = inputs[ "marks" ].unsqueeze( 0 ) inputs[ "num_options" ] = torch.tensor([[ len (questions[ 0 ].options)]]) inputs[ "question_type_ids" ] = torch.tensor([[ 1 ]]) # choice inputs[ "labels" ] = torch.tensor( [questions[ 0 ].options.index(label)] ) return inputs dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples] class DecisionTrainer ( Trainer ): def compute_loss ( self, model, inputs, return_outputs= False , **kwargs ): inputs = inputs.copy() labels = inputs.pop( "labels" ) logits = model(**inputs) logits = logits.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [3] -> [1, 3] loss = F.cross_entropy(logits. float (), labels) return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss trainer = DecisionTrainer( model=model, args=TrainingArguments( output_dir= "./decision-toy" , max_steps= 30 , per_device_train_batch_size= 1 , learning_rate= 1e-3 , logging_steps= 5 , save_strategy= "no" , report_to= "none" , remove_unused_columns= False , ), train_dataset=dataset, data_collator= lambda batch: batch[ 0 ], ) trainer.train() First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL ( huggingface/trl#8040 ), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open. If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head. Final thoughts Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software . Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.
