The source-node claim prevents local execution before the target node starts the command. 3.7 Results and Accounting The target node returns stdout, stderr, exit status, and cleanup information using the migrated command’s ID. The source node uses these results to finish the original CLI execution or shell tool call. Execution logs and local temporary files stay on the target node; workspace modifications are visible through shared storage. The command remains attributed to its owner instance, while per-node execution counts record where it actually runs. Batch elapsed time is measured at the submitting controller. The controlled experiments report queue waiting at both nodes; the agent traces report the broader submission-to-start interval defined in Section 5.6 . 4 Harbor Integration Harbor connects task specifications, coding agents, and automatic verification through the Metal Sandbox environment adapter. For each trial, the adapter creates an instance, uploads the task files, prepares the agent runtime within the instance, and starts the configured harness. The agent and verifier use separate execution phases; the verifier receives the completed workspace and returns the task result. Harbor retains these results and the agent trajectory for evaluation and rollout collection. Claude Code, Codex, and mini-SWE-agent are supported through the same managed command interface. Claude Code and Codex use tool hooks to route shell commands through the sandbox command helper. mini-SWE-agent uses its MetalEnvironment interface to submit commands and receive their outputs. Agent sessions run concurrently, and each tool call is scheduled independently. A migrated call retains its shell script, working directory, environment, and original result interface. Calls that lack a shared-workspace description remain on the owner node. Harbor task configuration selects the harness and runtime version, model endpoint, concurrency, and execution budgets. The adapter records command waiting separately from active execution, preserves stdout, stderr, and exit status, and collects the native trajectory and standardized ATIF record. This allows rollout timing to distinguish model requests, tool execution, and tool waiting. 5 Evaluation We measure command throughput, scaling with node count, and queue waiting under balanced and concentrated submissions, then examine longer commands and migration overhead. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.17316 (cs) [Submitted on 12 Nov 2026] Title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation Authors: Peiwen Li (Yale University), Harshit Verma (Yale University), Sophia Zhou (Yale University), Haiwen Wang (Yale University), Ngoc Bui (Yale University), Heng Chang (Tsinghua University), Fei Fei (Goodvision AI), David van Dijk (Yale University), Rex Ying (Yale University) View a PDF of the paper titled CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation, by Peiwen Li (Yale University) and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory. CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation Peiwen Li Affiliation: Yale University Harshit Verma Affiliation: Yale University Sophia Zhou Affiliation: Yale University Haiwen Wang Affiliation: Yale University Ngoc Bui Affiliation: Yale University Heng Chang Affiliation: Tsinghua University Fei Fei Affiliation: Goodvision AI * Equal contribution. Correspondence: peiwen.li@yale.edu David van Dijk Affiliation: Yale University Rex Ying Affiliation: Yale University Abstract Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Co ding- Re pository Mem ory ( CoReMem ) , a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors : repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor’s resolve rate from 21.0 % 21.0\% to 25.7 % 25.7\% , with 17 % 17\% fewer steps and 11 % 11\% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Memory on the next task. A memory written at the end of one flake8-simplify task hands two anchors, a location ( WHERE ) and a check ( VERIFY ), to the next task on the same repository; the post-trained actor model acts on them at steps 1 and 6 and skips the exploration it would otherwise start with (step counts illustrative). Figure 2: What crosses coding-task boundaries and where memory is valued and optimized. Existing settings keep memory within one task, transfer general experience across independent tasks, or carry memory while resetting the repository. Our setting carries both repository state and memory to unseen future tasks. The ↺ \circlearrowleft and ↓ \downarrow symbols indicate whether memory is valued and optimized on its source task or on future tasks. In real-world software development, coding agents are expected to handle successive tasks on an evolving repository. While prior research has primarily studied repository issues independently ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , recent work considers sequences of tasks on a shared, evolving repository ( Jin et al., 2026 ) . We study this successive-task setting, in which tasks arrive sequentially, each inherits the repository state left by earlier tasks, and future tasks are unknown in advance. Since this state carries over, suitable memory can let agents reuse information acquired during earlier exploration and avoid rediscovering it on unseen future tasks (Figure 1 ). We therefore consider both what a memory is worth and how an agent can use it to reduce the cost of solving unseen future tasks. Existing memory methods for coding agents are not specifically designed for the above successive-task setting and do not reliably save effort (steps and tokens) on unseen future tasks (Figure 3 ). As illustrated in Figure 2 , within-task methods learn to compact context for the current task, whose goal is already known ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026c ) . Most cross-task methods distill and transfer general experience and insights across independent tasks and repositories ( Ouyang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . MemOp instead accumulates memory across tasks within the same repository, but since the repository state is reset between tasks in its setting, it optimizes its memory design based on gains measured on the task that produced the memory ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , rather than on its value to an unseen future task that inherits the changed repository. Given these mismatches in setting and objective, Challenge 1 is to determine, before the future task is known, what information is worth carrying across the task boundary . Memory’s value is realized only when the actor model uses it appropriately during execution. Existing coding memory methods mainly optimize what is stored or retrieved, while typically leaving the model that reads it unchanged ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Yet an agent’s information needs evolve as a task unfolds ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) , making task-start retrieval insufficient to determine how memory should be used during execution. Challenge 2 is therefore how to use memory efficiently during execution to reduce the cost of solving unseen future tasks on the inherited repository . To address these challenges, we introduce Co ding- Re pository Mem ory ( CoReMem ), a cost-internalizing memory framework for successive coding tasks. Specifically, prospective segment valuation of memory addresses Challenge 1 by first formulating the prospective value of a memory at a task boundary, then valuing each part of the current task’s trajectory by what it saves on the next task, and from these values inducing, through a systematic procedure, a value-guided memory design for successive coding tasks. As a result, the value concentrates in anchors , references to repository locations and to executable checks, which later also mark the steps that act on the memory. To address Challenge 2, we propose on-policy adaptation for memory use with provenance-gated value credit, which adapts the actor model itself to act on the memory where that saves effort, in two steps. Cost-internalizing on-policy valuation trains the actor model in groups of rollouts with the memory, without it and with a misplaced memory, under a reward that charges steps inside success, so that the average gap between the rollouts with the memory and those without it exposes the memory’s value to the current actor model. For the rollouts that run with the memory, step-level provenance-gated value credit then pays the memory value to the steps whose anchors came from the memory, so that memory use is pushed by its measured value while every step keeps its outcome credit, and we show analytically that this push vanishes when the same value is paid to every step. Our contributions are summarized as follows. • We propose prospective segment valuation of memory, a systematic procedure that values each part of a trajectory by what it saves on the next task and induces a value-guided memory design for successive coding tasks. • We propose on-policy adaptation for memory use with provenance-gated value credit, which measures the memory value on-policy within each group of rollouts and passes the memory’s value directly to the steps that act on it. • On ChainSWE, a benchmark of successive tasks, CoReMem raises resolve per token over no memory by 41 % 41\% on average across three different actor models. 1 1 1 Code is available at an anonymous link . 2 Preliminaries Figure 3: Steps and tokens of each memory form against no memory. Hollow marks count only the acting model’s tokens, and the arrows add the tokens of the memory module. Parentheses give the relative change in resolve rate. The star is CoReMem w/o training (§ 3.1 ), the one form near the shaded quadrant where steps and total tokens both fall. In this paper, we consider a repository worked on by a chain of tasks T 1 , … , T K T_{1},\dots,T_{K} , carried out one after another in a single persistent workspace ( Jin et al., 2026 ) . Each task runs as its own session of an actor , the model that acts in the repository, which leaves the repository state S k S_{k} its edits produced and the trajectory τ k 	au_{k} of its actions and observations. At the boundary b k = ( S k , τ k , T k + 1 ) b_{k}=(S_{k},	au_{k},T_{k+1}) the state persists, since the next task opens the tree this one closed, while the trajectory is lost, and a memory m = π write ​ ( τ k ) m=\pi_{\mathrm{write}}(	au_{k}) , written once at the end of task k k and before T k + 1 T_{k+1} is issued, is the only text that crosses. Unlike cross-episode memory that resets each task to a base commit ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026a ) , the state here is inherited (Figure 2 ), so a memory cannot be checked on its own task, whose answer the repository holds. Does existing memory save effort? We run the existing forms of cross-task memory, the full history of the earlier tasks (App. B ), Mem0’s facts ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) , MemOp’s guidebook ( Guo et al., 2026 ) and ReasoningBank’s strategies ( Ouyang et al., 2026 ) , on the ChainSWE test set and count, for every form, the tokens of the acting model and of its memory module. Figure 3 places each by its change in steps and tokens against no memory, first with the acting model’s tokens alone and then adding the tokens of the memory module (Tables 1 and 3 have every number). Memory on successive tasks should lower the next task’s effort, its steps and the tokens they cost, yet no existing form reaches the quadrant where steps and total tokens both fall. Some buy resolution rather than effort, and each spends more tokens on its memory than it saves. Our aim is therefore a memory that lowers the effort of unseen future tasks without harming resolution, with what it keeps derived by valuing each part of a finished session by the effort it saves on these tasks and keeping what pays (§ 3.1 , the star in Figure 3 ). Learning objective. A memory can only point at what the next task should reuse, and effort is saved only when the actor acts on it. An actor is trained to solve a task from scratch rather than to read what an earlier task left, so it may pass over a memory that would spare it work or follow one that does not apply ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) , and whether a memory applies becomes clear only as the actor works through the task. (a) Prospective segment valuation of memory. A memory m m written from the trajectory τ k 	au_{k} is valued by the change Δ y ​ ( m ∣ b k ) \Delta_{y}(m\mid b_{k}) it causes on task k + 1 k{+}1 , run from the inherited tree S k S_{k} with and without m m . A group of G G sessions mixes sessions with their own memory ( m m ), no memory ( ∅ \varnothing ) and a misplaced memory ( m ~ 	ilde{m} ) under the reward R i R_{i} , and V ^ b = R ¯ m − R ¯ ∅ \widehat{V}_{b}= ar{R}_{m}- ar{R}_{\varnothing} is the memory’s value on-policy. CoReMem is cost-internalizing in the sense of Eq. ( 1 ). The effort a memory changes on the next task is measured, and that measurement enters both what the memory keeps and how the actor model is adapted to use it, in two parts (Figure 4 ). § 3.1 defines the value of a memory on unseen future tasks and lets it guide what the memory keeps, which turns out to be anchors. § 3.2 adapts the actor model to use that memory during execution, measuring the value again on-policy and paying it, through the anchors, to the steps that use the memory, on top of the outcome credit. 3.1 Prospective segment valuation of memory To decide, before the next task is known, what to carry across a task boundary, we provide a systematic procedure for inducing a memory design. We first define a memory’s prospective value on the next task, and use it to find which parts of a session’s history are worth carrying because they save effort on the next task. Prospective value of memory. CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation Peiwen Li Affiliation: Yale University Harshit Verma Affiliation: Yale University Sophia Zhou Affiliation: Yale University Haiwen Wang Affiliation: Yale University Ngoc Bui Affiliation: Yale University Heng Chang Affiliation: Tsinghua University Fei Fei Affiliation: Goodvision AI * Equal contribution. Correspondence: peiwen.li@yale.edu David van Dijk Affiliation: Yale University Rex Ying Affiliation: Yale University Abstract Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Co ding- Re pository Mem ory ( CoReMem ) , a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors : repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor’s resolve rate from 21.0 % 21.0\% to 25.7 % 25.7\% , with 17 % 17\% fewer steps and 11 % 11\% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Memory on the next task. A memory written at the end of one flake8-simplify task hands two anchors, a location ( WHERE ) and a check ( VERIFY ), to the next task on the same repository; the post-trained actor model acts on them at steps 1 and 6 and skips the exploration it would otherwise start with (step counts illustrative). Figure 2: What crosses coding-task boundaries and where memory is valued and optimized. Existing settings keep memory within one task, transfer general experience across independent tasks, or carry memory while resetting the repository. Our setting carries both repository state and memory to unseen future tasks. The ↺ \circlearrowleft and ↓ \downarrow symbols indicate whether memory is valued and optimized on its source task or on future tasks. In real-world software development, coding agents are expected to handle successive tasks on an evolving repository. While prior research has primarily studied repository issues independently ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , recent work considers sequences of tasks on a shared, evolving repository ( Jin et al., 2026 ) . We study this successive-task setting, in which tasks arrive sequentially, each inherits the repository state left by earlier tasks, and future tasks are unknown in advance. Since this state carries over, suitable memory can let agents reuse information acquired during earlier exploration and avoid rediscovering it on unseen future tasks (Figure 1 ). We therefore consider both what a memory is worth and how an agent can use it to reduce the cost of solving unseen future tasks. Existing memory methods for coding agents are not specifically designed for the above successive-task setting and do not reliably save effort (steps and tokens) on unseen future tasks (Figure 3 ). As illustrated in Figure 2 , within-task methods learn to compact context for the current task, whose goal is already known ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026c ) . Most cross-task methods distill and transfer general experience and insights across independent tasks and repositories ( Ouyang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . MemOp instead accumulates memory across tasks within the same repository, but since the repository state is reset between tasks in its setting, it optimizes its memory design based on gains measured on the task that produced the memory ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , rather than on its value to an unseen future task that inherits the changed repository. Given these mismatches in setting and objective, Challenge 1 is to determine, before the future task is known, what information is worth carrying across the task boundary . Memory’s value is realized only when the actor model uses it appropriately during execution. Existing coding memory methods mainly optimize what is stored or retrieved, while typically leaving the model that reads it unchanged ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Yet an agent’s information needs evolve as a task unfolds ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) , making task-start retrieval insufficient to determine how memory should be used during execution. Challenge 2 is therefore how to use memory efficiently during execution to reduce the cost of solving unseen future tasks on the inherited repository . To address these challenges, we introduce Co ding- Re pository Mem ory ( CoReMem ), a cost-internalizing memory framework for successive coding tasks. Specifically, prospective segment valuation of memory addresses Challenge 1 by first formulating the prospective value of a memory at a task boundary, then valuing each part of the current task’s trajectory by what it saves on the next task, and from these values inducing, through a systematic procedure, a value-guided memory design for successive coding tasks. As a result, the value concentrates in anchors , references to repository locations and to executable checks, which later also mark the steps that act on the memory. To address Challenge 2, we propose on-policy adaptation for memory use with provenance-gated value credit, which adapts the actor model itself to act on the memory where that saves effort, in two steps. Cost-internalizing on-policy valuation trains the actor model in groups of rollouts with the memory, without it and with a misplaced memory, under a reward that charges steps inside success, so that the average gap between the rollouts with the memory and those without it exposes the memory’s value to the current actor model. For the rollouts that run with the memory, step-level provenance-gated value credit then pays the memory value to the steps whose anchors came from the memory, so that memory use is pushed by its measured value while every step keeps its outcome credit, and we show analytically that this push vanishes when the same value is paid to every step. R. Whittington View a PDF of the paper titled Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models, by Benjamin Hoover and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques. Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000 × 	imes Faster than Looped Models Benjamin Hoover 1 Hugh Blayney 1 James C. R. Whittington 1 Abstract Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank’s energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM , solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000 × {	imes} faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282 × {	imes} fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques. † † footnotetext: 1 Prefrontal, London, United Kingdom. Correspondence to Benjamin Hoover <ben@prefrontal.ai> , James C.R. Whittington <james@prefrontal.ai> 1 Introduction Figure 1: CRAM learns an energy from solved puzzles in seconds, and the energy tells the search when to stop. Training (left) pulls down the energy of each solution and pushes up the energy of negative samples, without differentiating through a reasoning trajectory (shown is a pseudolikelihood objective, Eq. 5 ). On one H200, training takes 42 ms on Sudoku-Extreme and 132 ms on Maze-Unique, at least 1,000 × {	imes} faster than the looped models of Table 2 . Reasoning (right) clamps the clues of a new puzzle, starts several chains from random fills of the other cells (light-blue guesses; one board per chain), and minimizes the energy one cell at a time, using at least 282 × {	imes} fewer inference FLOPs ( Fig. 2 ) than looped models at matched accuracy. The chains are independent, and the descent can be noisy, which lets a chain escape spurious local minima. The search stops when any chain’s energy falls below a stopping threshold fitted from the training solutions. An emerging new paradigm for reasoning is looping, in which a layer, or block of layers, is repeatedly applied to produce an answer. Small looped models [ 62 , 38 ] (millions of parameters) have had successes on simple benchmarks such as Sudoku and mazes. However, they are slow to train in part due to their use of truncated backprop-through-time (BPTT), and the reasons behind their successes remain unclear [ 2 , 51 ] . Energy minimization is a related framework that offers a principled approach to looping. Here, each loop step corresponds to a gradient descent step on an energy function. Minimizing energy offers many potential benefits, such as guaranteed stability, early stopping, and efficient training methods that bypass the need for BPTT. Indeed, looped reasoners have begun adopting the ideas of energy-based networks without adopting an explicit energy. Some train their updates to converge to attractors or fixed points, a guarantee intrinsic to energy network dynamics [ 36 , 44 ] . Others learn when to stop with a separate halting network [ 28 , 5 , 62 , 38 ] . Each of these desirable properties is generally added on top of the looped network through an extra head, loss, or module, and the network is trained by backpropagating through its repeated applications. With looped models rebuilding the desirable properties of an energy one at a time, we ask: why not learn the energy directly? It’s already known that constraint puzzles like Sudoku have a corresponding energy that, when minimized, solves the puzzle [ 34 ] . In the 1980’s, Hopfield and Tank showed how to hand-design an energy function that solves certain classes of logic problems [ 35 ] . It is, however, less well understood if an explicit energy can be learned from data to solve a wide array of reasoning problems. Here, we develop a trainable version of the Hopfield-Tank energy and then learn the weights directly from puzzles. We call this tiny trainable energy, together with the recurrent dynamics that descend it at inference time, a Compact Reasoning Associative Memory ( CRAM ).We call it this because, as in a Hopfield network [ 32 ] , its weights memorize associations between pairs of valid cells, and descent on the energy completes a corrupted pattern (i.e., a puzzle provided with only its clues). CRAM ’s energy is a special case of the energies of modern Hopfield networks [ 40 , 41 ] . In this work we: 1) show that CRAM trains at least 1,000 × {	imes} faster than modern looped models and reasons with at least 282 × {	imes} fewer inference FLOPs on a variety of different puzzles (Sudoku-Extreme [ 62 ] , Maze-Unique [ 36 ] , and the N-Queens and graph-coloring sets of Baek et al. [3] ); 2) show that CRAM provides a stopping test that allows compute to scale with the difficulty of a puzzle; 3) show that CRAM is data-efficient, learning interpretable weights from Sudoku-Extreme using an order of magnitude fewer training puzzles than looped models; 4) show that local training objectives train fastest compared to other methods of training the same energy — significantly faster than BPTT; and 5) show that a hand-set CRAM energy with few unique weights can solve every test puzzle from every benchmark exactly. CRAM represents the state of the art on speed and efficiency of looping to solve constraint puzzles, by several orders of magnitude. However, since these puzzles can be solved easily with so few parameters using CRAM , our work suggests that high accuracy on these benchmarks are not indicative of future performance on harder tasks. Indeed, CRAM ’s simple energy on its own would struggle to learn more complex reasoning tasks like ARC-AGI [ 12 ] , though we do show how a simple latent extension of CRAM can solve Maze-Hard near perfectly in App. F . Nevertheless, the dramatic speed-up that this energy provides on the presented tasks offers a potential path forward for data-efficient general reasoning capabilities. 2 Background CRAM ’s energy is a form of pairwise graphical model in that it is a sum of costs on and between cells, as in the energy of a Markov random field (MRF) [ 7 , 61 ] . Learning these costs goes by several names, such as constraint programming [ 54 ] or constraint acquisition [ 9 , 6 , 15 ] . Recent methods show that you can learn pairwise costs for Sudoku directly from solved puzzles, using approximate likelihood methods like those studied in this work [ 10 , 16 , 17 ] . However, to infer solutions to new puzzles, these methods pass the learned constraints to an external solver [ 13 ] . CRAM keeps this learning problem but uses neural optimization methods to replace the external solver with recurrent search on its own energy [ 35 , 47 ] . Energy-based networks treat an energy over a large search space of possible solutions as the objective of both training and inference. Training shapes the energy to be low at observed data; inference or “reasoning” minimizes the energy to sample low-energy solutions (see Fig. 1 ) [ 32 , 42 ] . Hopfield and Tank used a version of the Hopfield Network with continuous neurons to solve constraint problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem with hand-set weights [ 33 , 35 ] , and later work did the same for Sudoku [ 34 ] . CRAM writes these energies in a mean-field free energy form with learnable weights [ 47 ] . This form approximates the free energy of a Boltzmann machine, which have similarly been applied to logic and combinatorial problems [ 1 , 30 , 14 , 59 ] . However, none of these energies have been trained by observing puzzle solutions alone. Modern looped reasoners use deep, weight-tied networks to learn puzzles directly from data. HRM and TRM popularized this design for Sudoku, mazes and ARC, building on recurrent relational networks and universal transformers [ 62 , 38 , 12 , 46 , 18 ] . Later works varied the architecture but kept the same training approach: backpropagating through the reasoning trajectory of a depth-recurrent model to refine the model’s prediction for a specified input [ 25 , 3 , 55 , 24 , 64 , 39 , 57 , 52 ] . Some approaches use diffusion- and flow-style training to avoid BPTT [ 21 , 64 , 39 , 29 , 65 , 57 ] . Others engineer fixed point behavior into deep models, training the update loop to converge to stable equilibria [ 36 , 44 , 29 , 65 , 23 ] . This last direction holds promise, since Hopfield & Tank already showed that these reasoning puzzles are naturally suited to fixed-point problems. Energy-based looped models encourage convergence by training an energy on top of a deep network, seeking to combine the best of looped models with advantages of Hopfield Networks and Boltzmann Machines [ 20 , 21 , 27 , 43 , 49 , 66 , 11 ] . For example, concurrent work Energy-Based Reasoners (EBR) [ 11 ] showcases several advantages of energy for looped model reasoning: it trains an energy on the latent states of a TRM-style transformer, descends it with noisy projected gradient steps, and stops when the gradient norm is small [ 11 ] . Though similar in spirit, these networks are much larger and slower than CRAM , and all of them learn through BPTT. 3 Method The reasoning tasks studied in this work can be represented via M M answer variables called cells , each with up to C C candidate values. Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000 × 	imes Faster than Looped Models Benjamin Hoover 1 Hugh Blayney 1 James C. R. Whittington 1 Abstract Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank’s energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM , solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000 × {	imes} faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282 × {	imes} fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques. † † footnotetext: 1 Prefrontal, London, United Kingdom. Correspondence to Benjamin Hoover <ben@prefrontal.ai> , James C.R. Whittington <james@prefrontal.ai> 1 Introduction Figure 1: CRAM learns an energy from solved puzzles in seconds, and the energy tells the search when to stop. Training (left) pulls down the energy of each solution and pushes up the energy of negative samples, without differentiating through a reasoning trajectory (shown is a pseudolikelihood objective, Eq. 5 ). On one H200, training takes 42 ms on Sudoku-Extreme and 132 ms on Maze-Unique, at least 1,000 × {	imes} faster than the looped models of Table 2 . Reasoning (right) clamps the clues of a new puzzle, starts several chains from random fills of the other cells (light-blue guesses; one board per chain), and minimizes the energy one cell at a time, using at least 282 × {	imes} fewer inference FLOPs ( Fig. 2 ) than looped models at matched accuracy. The chains are independent, and the descent can be noisy, which lets a chain escape spurious local minima. The search stops when any chain’s energy falls below a stopping threshold fitted from the training solutions. An emerging new paradigm for reasoning is looping, in which a layer, or block of layers, is repeatedly applied to produce an answer. Small looped models [ 62 , 38 ] (millions of parameters) have had successes on simple benchmarks such as Sudoku and mazes. However, they are slow to train in part due to their use of truncated backprop-through-time (BPTT), and the reasons behind their successes remain unclear [ 2 , 51 ] . Energy minimization is a related framework that offers a principled approach to looping. Here, each loop step corresponds to a gradient descent step on an energy function. Minimizing energy offers many potential benefits, such as guaranteed stability, early stopping, and efficient training methods that bypass the need for BPTT. Indeed, looped reasoners have begun adopting the ideas of energy-based networks without adopting an explicit energy. Some train their updates to converge to attractors or fixed points, a guarantee intrinsic to energy network dynamics [ 36 , 44 ] . Others learn when to stop with a separate halting network [ 28 , 5 , 62 , 38 ] . Each of these desirable properties is generally added on top of the looped network through an extra head, loss, or module, and the network is trained by backpropagating through its repeated applications. With looped models rebuilding the desirable properties of an energy one at a time, we ask: why not learn the energy directly? It’s already known that constraint puzzles like Sudoku have a corresponding energy that, when minimized, solves the puzzle [ 34 ] . In the 1980’s, Hopfield and Tank showed how to hand-design an energy function that solves certain classes of logic problems [ 35 ] . It is, however, less well understood if an explicit energy can be learned from data to solve a wide array of reasoning problems. Here, we develop a trainable version of the Hopfield-Tank energy and then learn the weights directly from puzzles. We call this tiny trainable energy, together with the recurrent dynamics that descend it at inference time, a Compact Reasoning Associative Memory ( CRAM ).We call it this because, as in a Hopfield network [ 32 ] , its weights memorize associations between pairs of valid cells, and descent on the energy completes a corrupted pattern (i.e., a puzzle provided with only its clues). CRAM ’s energy is a special case of the energies of modern Hopfield networks [ 40 , 41 ] . In this work we: 1) show that CRAM trains at least 1,000 × {	imes} faster than modern looped models and reasons with at least 282 × {	imes} fewer inference FLOPs on a variety of different puzzles (Sudoku-Extreme [ 62 ] , Maze-Unique [ 36 ] , and the N-Queens and graph-coloring sets of Baek et al. [3] ); 2) show that CRAM provides a stopping test that allows compute to scale with the difficulty of a puzzle; 3) show that CRAM is data-efficient, learning interpretable weights from Sudoku-Extreme using an order of magnitude fewer training puzzles than looped models; 4) show that local training objectives train fastest compared to other methods of training the same energy — significantly faster than BPTT; and 5) show that a hand-set CRAM energy with few unique weights can solve every test puzzle from every benchmark exactly. CRAM represents the state of the art on speed and efficiency of looping to solve constraint puzzles, by several orders of magnitude. However, since these puzzles can be solved easily with so few parameters using CRAM , our work suggests that high accuracy on these benchmarks are not indicative of future performance on harder tasks. Indeed, CRAM ’s simple energy on its own would struggle to learn more complex reasoning tasks like ARC-AGI [ 12 ] , though we do show how a simple latent extension of CRAM can solve Maze-Hard near perfectly in App. F . Nevertheless, the dramatic speed-up that this energy provides on the presented tasks offers a potential path forward for data-efficient general reasoning capabilities. 2 Background CRAM ’s energy is a form of pairwise graphical model in that it is a sum of costs on and between cells, as in the energy of a Markov random field (MRF) [ 7 , 61 ] . Learning these costs goes by several names, such as constraint programming [ 54 ] or constraint acquisition [ 9 , 6 , 15 ] . Recent methods show that you can learn pairwise costs for Sudoku directly from solved puzzles, using approximate likelihood methods like those studied in this work [ 10 , 16 , 17 ] . However, to infer solutions to new puzzles, these methods pass the learned constraints to an external solver [ 13 ] . CRAM keeps this learning problem but uses neural optimization methods to replace the external solver with recurrent search on its own energy [ 35 , 47 ] . Energy-based networks treat an energy over a large search space of possible solutions as the objective of both training and inference. Training shapes the energy to be low at observed data; inference or “reasoning” minimizes the energy to sample low-energy solutions (see Fig. 1 ) [ 32 , 42 ] . Hopfield and Tank used a version of the Hopfield Network with continuous neurons to solve constraint problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem with hand-set weights [ 33 , 35 ] , and later work did the same for Sudoku [ 34 ] . CRAM writes these energies in a mean-field free energy form with learnable weights [ 47 ] . This form approximates the free energy of a Boltzmann machine, which have similarly been applied to logic and combinatorial problems [ 1 , 30 , 14 , 59 ] . However, none of these energies have been trained by observing puzzle solutions alone. Modern looped reasoners use deep, weight-tied networks to learn puzzles directly from data. HRM and TRM popularized this design for Sudoku, mazes and ARC, building on recurrent relational networks and universal transformers [ 62 , 38 , 12 , 46 , 18 ] . Later works varied the architecture but kept the same training approach: backpropagating through the reasoning trajectory of a depth-recurrent model to refine the model’s prediction for a specified input [ 25 , 3 , 55 , 24 , 64 , 39 , 57 , 52 ] . Some approaches use diffusion- and flow-style training to avoid BPTT [ 21 , 64 , 39 , 29 , 65 , 57 ] . Others engineer fixed point behavior into deep models, training the update loop to converge to stable equilibria [ 36 , 44 , 29 , 65 , 23 ] . This last direction holds promise, since Hopfield & Tank already showed that these reasoning puzzles are naturally suited to fixed-point problems. Energy-based looped models encourage convergence by training an energy on top of a deep network, seeking to combine the best of looped models with advantages of Hopfield Networks and Boltzmann Machines [ 20 , 21 , 27 , 43 , 49 , 66 , 11 ] . For example, concurrent work Energy-Based Reasoners (EBR) [ 11 ] showcases several advantages of energy for looped model reasoning: it trains an energy on the latent states of a TRM-style transformer, descends it with noisy projected gradient steps, and stops when the gradient norm is small [ 11 ] . Though similar in spirit, these networks are much larger and slower than CRAM , and all of them learn through BPTT. 3 Method The reasoning tasks studied in this work can be represented via M M answer variables called cells , each with up to C C candidate values. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.17267 (cs) [Submitted on 12 Nov 2026] Title: LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds Authors: Pengcheng Zhou , Xuanyu Liu , Yanchen Yin , Tianjie Ju , Bobo Li , Shengqiong Wu , Hao Fei , Mong-Li Lee , Wynne Hsu View a PDF of the paper titled LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds, by Pengcheng Zhou and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic environments using GeoWorld. Unlike existing evaluations that largely reason and plan over fixed geographic states, GeoWorld is grounded in real-world geographic structure and allows external world states to evolve along their own temporal processes while preserving verifiable state histories. LiveGeo places geographic tasks within this evolving environment, requiring agents to actively acquire task-relevant information, verify whether the evidence supporting prior decisions remains valid, and revise their plans when necessary. Our results reveal that even frontier LLMs struggle with static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, while strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability. Further analysis identifies a key bottleneck: agents struggle to acquire and translate relevant evidence into valid decisions and maintain their correctness as the world evolves. By releasing LiveGeo together with its GeoWorld platform, we aim to provide the community with a flexible and extensible infrastructure for studying the next generation of agents capable of reliable action in evolving geographic worlds. items.title: master-2026-11-07: chore: remove leading newlines in module doc-strings (#45739)
items.summary:
Per mathlib's style guide, module doc-strings are not supposed to begin with a leading newline. About 600 files in mathlib violate this. This also causes spurious diffs in the verso doc-string migration (see #45730).

As a by-product, we also remove a few leading newlines in section header doc-strings: they need not be present either, and not removing them would be more work that it's worth.

This PR was generated purely mechanically by replacing the regex /-! with /-! within VS Code.

This rate replaces that for adjustment credit, which was discontinued after January 8, 2003. For further information, see www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/press/bcreg/2002/200210312/default.htm . From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 13, 2026 Back to Top
